name: Cole Train (Cole Train Apartments)
award: 2025 Federal 4% and state housing tax credits (Round Two)
headline: Medici Development plans Cole Train, a four-story brick building with 63 apartments for households at 30% to 60% AMI, on a vacant part of the Urban Land Conservancy's Tramway Nonprofit Center block at 1675 E. 35th Avenue in Denver's Cole neighborhood. It won 2025 Round Two federal 4%, state and TOC credits from CHFA.
why_it_matters: It shows a community land trust deal: ULC keeps the land and leases it to the developer, affordability is set for at least 99 years, and residents get services from the nonprofits next door; it needed a contested PUD rezoning, which Council passed unanimously on 2026-02-23.

status.label: Credits awarded and site rezoned; construction not started
status.detail: Denver City Council passed the rezoning (CB25-1069, PUD-G 38) on 2026-02-23. In March 2026 ULC said groundbreaking is planned for early 2027 with opening in late 2027 or early 2028. No public record of a closing, building permit or groundbreaking was found as of 2026-10-21.

next_step: Watch for a Denver City Council HOST loan resolution, building permits for 1675 E. 35th Avenue, and the CHFA bond closing ahead of the planned early 2027 groundbreaking.

key_numbers.meaning: 8 studios, 29 one-bedroom, 22 two-bedroom and 4 three-bedroom units at 30%, 40%, 50% and 60% AMI.
About $8.9M over 10 years, plus $1,108,901 accelerated state credit and $81,900 TOC credit.
CHFA is the bond issuer; the application planned $12.0M of tax-exempt bonds plus $4.0M taxable, privately placed with ANB Bank.
ULC keeps the land in its community land trust for at least 99 years and Medici leases it; the city's Affordable Housing Plan also carries a 99-year covenant.

facts.value: 1675 E. 35th Avenue, Denver 80205 (northwest corner of Gilpin Street and 35th Avenue)
Four stories of wood frame, one elevator, interior corridors, mainly brick exterior to match the historic Tramway building, post-tensioned slab
71 units an acre, per the application
50 on-site stalls, some shared with Tramway staff by day; residents may use ULC's lot across Gilpin Street in the evening

Route 38 on Bruce Randolph Boulevard (every 15 minutes) one block south, Route 12 on Downing two blocks west, and the 38th and Blake A Line station about seven blocks west. The operating budget includes RTD EcoPasses
All-electric and solar-ready, certifying to the DOE Efficient New Homes (formerly Zero Energy Ready Homes) program; the application also targets Enterprise Green Communities 2020
Rezoned from R-MU-20 with waivers and PUD 534 to PUD-G 38 (application 2024I-00122). Subarea B, the housing site, allows only multi-unit homes up to 4 stories and 45 feet
Phillips Center LLC; ULC was the rezoning applicant
The Tramway Nonprofit Center, a former Denver Tramway Company bus and streetcar building on the State and National Registers, housing more than 15 nonprofits
Priority for Cole residents recently displaced or at risk of displacement

money.source: Colorado accelerated state housing tax credit

money.note: The applicant says the TOC equity lowers debt enough to pay for EcoPasses.
CHFA is the issuer. The application planned $12.0M of tax-exempt bonds to meet the 50% test, $4.0M of taxable construction bonds and a $5.6M permanent loan, privately placed with ANB Bank.

The application names city and state loans without amounts; ULC says the project has affordability agreements with CHFA and Denver HOST. No Denver City Council loan resolution was found as of 2026-10-21.
ULC keeps the land; Medici owns the building and leases the land.

background.text: Medici and ULC built Walnut Flats about half a mile away (opened 2020) and also worked together on Evans Station.
ULC began community meetings on the vacant parcel in 2018; residents named affordable housing as their top choice for the site.

The project was a use by right under the old zoning, but ULC sought a custom PUD to protect the Tramway building, remove a 10,000 sq ft office cap and allow the housing. Planning Board recommended approval 7-0 on 2025-07-16.

The council committee step set for 2025-07-29 was postponed for mediation with some Cole residents, which centered on the four-story height. ULC offered shared parking, resident amenities, priority for displaced Cole residents and community use of the Tramway building, which did not resolve every concern.

A protest petition filed 2026-02-17 reached 19.7% of nearby land area, short of the 20% needed to require a council supermajority. Council passed the rezoning unanimously on 2026-02-23 after 33 speakers in support and four opposed.
ULC signed an Affordable Housing Plan with HOST: if the tax credit project is not built, any apartments on the site must be 100% at or below 80% AMI for 99 years, with no fee-in-lieu.
The project is in Denver's Affordable Housing Review Team (Proposition 123 fast-track) review.
DOLA confirmed the site is in a Transit-Oriented Communities transit area under HB24-1313.
The applicant's market study found rents at least 14% below Class B market comparables and an 18% capture rate, and the applicant did not request a basis boost.
BusinessDen's $2.1 million in tax credits matches the combined CHFA federal, state and TOC awards (inferred from the sums).

discrepancies.text: The application says the housing parcel is about 38,000 sq ft, slightly over half an acre, while Naked Denver describes a 0.84-acre site and BusinessDen says ULC is leasing 2.3 acres to Medici.
The application says ULC acquired the Tramway building in 2017, while ULC says it has owned and operated the Tramway Nonprofit Center since 2007.
BusinessDen reported in February 2026 that construction was expected to begin in 2026, while ULC said in March 2026 that groundbreaking is planned for early 2027.
CHFA's award report shows $6,720,000 in bonds, while the application planned $12.0 million of tax-exempt bonds plus $4.0 million taxable.
The application describes the Tramway building as 65,000 sq ft, the city staff report as about 63,000 sq ft of office, and BusinessDen as 60,000 sq ft.
